scenes.narration: Look up on a clear day, and the sky is blue. But sunlight itself is white. So where does the blue come from?
scenes.visualIntent: Full-bleed day-sky gradient with title text WHY IS THE SKY BLUE

scenes.narration: The answer is written in the air itself. Tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, far smaller than a wave of light.
scenes.visualIntent: Sun rays entering a field of molecule dots
scenes.onScreenText: THE AIR IS FULL OF MOLECULES

scenes.narration: When sunlight hits them, they scatter short blue wavelengths in every direction, several times more strongly than red. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from everywhere overhead. That is why the whole sky glows blue.
scenes.visualIntent: Ray hits molecule, blue rays fan out; spectrum bar highlights blue

scenes.assetRequirement: spectrum bar with violet dimmed, eye hint
scenes.narration: Violet is scattered even more, but there is less of it in sunlight, and your eyes are less sensitive to it.
scenes.visualIntent: Spectrum bar, violet segment dimmed, simple eye glyph

scenes.narration: At sunset, sunlight crosses much more air. The blue is scattered away, and the reds and oranges remain.
scenes.visualIntent: Low sun, long slanted path arrow through atmosphere band, orange horizon

scenes.narration: Dust and pollution scatter all colors equally, which is why a hazy sky looks pale and white. So the blue sky is not a thing. It is sunlight, rearranged by the air. Thanks for watching.
scenes.visualIntent: Split pale haze panel, then closing card SUNLIGHT, REARRANGED
